title: Buffered vs Unbuffered Channels in Go

scenes.say: Ever wonder when to use a buffered channel instead of an unbuffered one? Let’s break down why it matters.

scenes.label: Unbuffered
scenes.sub: Blocks sender until a receiver is ready.
scenes.say: An unbuffered channel blocks the sender until a receiver is ready. This means both sides must sync up every time.

scenes.label: Buffered
scenes.sub: Lets you send up to its capacity without blocking.
scenes.say: A buffered channel lets you send messages up to its capacity without waiting. The sender only blocks when the buffer is full.

scenes.code:
ch := make(chan int, 2)
ch <- 1
ch <- 2 // no block yet
scenes.say: Here, we create a channel with room for two messages. Sending two values won’t block until the buffer fills up.
Unbuffered channels are synchronous—sender and receiver must meet. Buffered channels are asynchronous, so the sender can get ahead.

scenes.question: What can cause deadlocks with buffers?
scenes.right: If the buffer fills up and no receiver drains it, your program can still deadlock.
scenes.say: Here’s a trap: buffered channels don’t magically prevent deadlocks. If the buffer fills and nothing reads from it, you’re stuck.
